utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning. Mr. President, there was filed this morning an addendum to the expedited -- actually, I should go into private session before I discuss this first issue, if we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Could the Chamber move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'll repeat. Judge Lattanzi is indisposed today and we'll be sitting for the first session pursuant to Rule 15 bis. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I just wanted to briefly raise the latest expression of the ongoing and frankly massive disclosure violation by the -- violations by the Defence related to the provision of information under the Rules and the guidance in this particular case as well for information related to witnesses who are due to testify. In this case, in this instance, the Prosecution received considerable additional information about the witness -- I'll get his KDZ number, well Mr. Indjic, in any event, comprising lengthy commentary, about 21 newly notified documents, 15 of which were not on the 65 ter list and three of which are not translated. So those create significant problems by way of preparation, as the Court can imagine. Ms. Edgerton is here to provide any additional details since she is deeply immersed in the particulars of the preparation and the documents. I would note, however, that the nature of the problem is such that Mr. Robinson also appreciates the difficulties which arise from that belated notification and has indicated, for example, that he had no objection to the deferral of Mr. Indjic's cross-examination until at least some point after Mr. Milosevic's examination-in-chief. And I appreciate his acknowledgement of the difficulties that arise, although as the Court is aware we are seeing this on a -- now a fairly regular basis. I can provide the Court or Ms. Edgerton can provide the Court with any additional details that may be required, but it is safe to say that the late notification presents hurdles that need to be addressed and that we ask the Court to attend to. I would also note that in accordance with the Court's practice in terms of late notification of materials related to a 92 ter submission, that we would expect a minimum of course that those would be led live, but as we discussed last week the requirement or the expectation that parties will lead information belatedly noticed live is separate from the issue of resolving the notice problem. So I address those in two different -- I compartmentalise those for purposes of addressing the Court and as I did in my discussion with Mr. Robinson. So those are two remedies that come to mind. The Court may have other matters in mind and I know the Court has indicated in the past it might impose more Draconian solutions rather than the practical solution of leading matters live and deferring cross-examination until such time as the Prosecution can at least have the hope of properly preparing. But at this moment we're seeking only that those matters be led live and that the cross-examination be deferred until we can satisfactorily prepare to deal with the material provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. First of all, our position is really unequivocal in the sense that we don't mind the Prosecution having enough time to prepare and recognise that when they receive new information, such as they have over the weekend, that they should be entitled to whatever time they reasonably need to prepare before commencing their cross-examination. On the other hand, we don't think there's any violation of the Court's rules and the circumstances of Mr. Indjic's statement is pretty much as follows: First of all, he was interviewed I believe in 2011. You recall that the Court continually admonished us that we should be preparing our Defence case during the Prosecution case, so we tried to do that. And so we took a statement from him back then. And then when he came for proofing over the weekend Dr. Karadzic elicited further information that he thought was important and that had since 2011 been highlighted as being of importance to us. And so that's why all those paragraphs and 20 documents were added to the statement during -- immediately after the proofing and notified to the Prosecution over the weekend. So the rule essentially requires us to make our 92 ter package 48 hours in advance of the witness's testimony. That witness will probably commence his direct examination this afternoon, but the cross-examination wouldn't have commenced until tomorrow morning. So we would have been within the 48 hours and I think that we've given enough notice. We disclosed the documents to the Prosecution earlier than this weekend. I think we'd given them those documents about at least a week ago if not more. So we've done everything we could to comply with the rules, and I think we have, and on the other hand we recognise the Prosecution should have sufficient time to deal with this kind of volume of new material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, would you like to add anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Essentially, Mr. President, as you've seen, Mr. Robinson's submission is consistent with the solution proposed by the Prosecution in this particular case; nevertheless, I think I have to address the suggestion that whatever materials are provided 48 hours in advance satisfy the rules or standards imposed by this Court. It is obvious that there is a stretching and then a breaking point to the amount of material that can be provided immediately before the 48-hour dead-line that essentially crosses the pragmatic line established by the Court, and there was reference to that earlier. And the Court always referred to the issue of the extent of the material provided and the nature of that material. So while I'm -- I don't know that it implicates a specific issue by way of resolution in this instance, it's important I think for the Defence to continue to bear in mind that the nature of the material added, the volume of the material added, can run afoul of the guidance provided by the Court if it is extensive enough irrespective of whether it technically is provided before the 48-hour dead-line. And you can look at that in different ways. You can think of it being a completely different statement or you could simply heed the Court's repeated admonitions in earlier portions of the case. But the fact is if the -- if either party has in mind a great deal of additional information that wasn't notified previously, they simply have to deal with that in other ways rather than dumping it on the other party at the last moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, the Chamber wasn't aware of this situation. I just received an e-mail from my staff that -- stating that the Chamber has received this revised statement at 9.30 p.m. on Saturday, and the Chamber hasn't had any opportunity to look through whether this is -- this -- these additional associated exhibits would form the part -- indispensable and inseparable part of the statement. I'll consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, being consistent with the Chamber's practice, the Chamber will order the Defence to lead live with respect to any revised part -- added part as well as the associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, would the Chamber consider allowing us to vary the order of witnesses so that the direct examination of Mr. Indjic occurs after the direct examination of Dragomir Milosevic, thus giving the Chamber at least a couple of days to look over the new material and the new documents? I should also indicate that we disclosed the documents 29th of November to the Prosecution that we thought we might be using, including these 20, of which three are untranslated. And we recognise we would either have to lead those live or abandon them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: A few things, Mr. President. First of all, let me point out and on a very practical level that the same counsel, Ms. Edgerton, is -- will be cross-examining both witnesses in this case. So the change of order doesn't address the preparation issue for us. That implicates a second comment I wanted to make, which is we understand the Court's guidance, consistent guidance, that belatedly notified material needs to be led live as a reflection of the fact the Court does not consider that an appropriate usage of 92 ter and therefore reverts back to the more conventional manner of leading evidence. But of course it doesn't address the preparation issue. Either way we've just received that information and it creates the same problem so we need to resolve that as well, which I think is reflected in Mr. Robinson's comments. But as I say, in this instance it doesn't seem to accomplish that. And finally, the provision of the documents relatively shortly before but untethered to anything by way of notification about what role they play in the context of the witness's testimony is of course more welcome than not providing them at all, but of only the most modest assistance to the Prosecution in properly preparing. We are not looking for ways to gum-up the process, Mr. President. We have bent over backwards to try to accommodate that and our lawyers are working deep into the night as a result of these belated notifications to be as prepared as possible. So when we bring these matters to the attention of the Court, it's because it presents significant preparation obstacle, one that I think is actually quite clear, both to the parties and to the Bench.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say a couple of words, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not wish to go back to that, but I wish to remind you of one thing. I asked to start on the 1st of March and that was a realistic assessment. On the other hand, no one can really know that well what a witness can say as I can. Here we have the accused and we have the lead counsel for Defence in detention. As for the witness's knowledge, the extent of his knowledge, I only got to know about that during proofing. Very often witnesses are proofed via videolink which can have a huge detrimental effect on the fairness and legality of this -- of these proceedings. I am trying to contribute as much as I can myself. We are a lot fewer than the Prosecution. We work until the wee hours of the morning, sometimes 4.00 or 5.00 in the morning. We're dropping --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- because we're tired. By the 1st of March we will have gone through over a hundred witnesses and we will be very tired by that time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, by leading live some part of a certain witness, what prejudice do you have at all?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No prejudice, Mr. President, so long as you grant us additional hours over the 300 to accommodate that, then we would have no prejudice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given the significance or importance of this witness, this witness could have been ordered to be led live. So I think it's a good way to strike a balance to lead live with respect to the revised and added part, and it's only -- it relates only 20 documents. I'll consult my colleagues again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber sees no reason to revise its ruling it gave earlier on. Shall we bring in the witness? But next witness is Pljevaljcic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah, Mr. President, just if I may by way of clarification. Given Mr. Robinson's initial acknowledgement of the problem and acquiescence in the suggestion that the cross-examination of Mr. Indjic be deferred until after the Dragomir Milosevic direct examination, it may have been that the Court considered that that was an agreed approach and didn't articulate it, but I just wanted to confirm for the sake of certainty of scheduling that that would be the approach adopted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We're still willing to do that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As to the order of witnesses, I would leave it to the parties if it is convenient. The Chamber sees no difficulty with it. Let's see how it evolves. And -- yes. Would the witness take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pljevaljcic. Make yourself comfortable, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, will it be you to have the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But the Chamber hasn't been informed of the time for cross, but I take it the Prosecution understands that in case of viva voce witness the Prosecution will have the same amount of time as the Defence for its evidence in chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Excellencies. Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Pljevaljcic.

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: Good morning, and I'm wishing you all the best.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As you have learned, perhaps we have to have this examination-in-chief viva voce, so we will go through all the steps. Could you please tell us your first, last name, and your father's name?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: I'm Trivko Pljevaljcic, son of Milo, born in 1955 in the municipality of Foca, former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I made a mistake now. I began too early. We need to pause between question and answer. Can you please tell us what your education is.

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: I completed secondary school as an electrical engineer and this is what I did my whole life.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you serve in the army?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what was your speciality?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: I served in the communications section.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And where did you work and what were your duties?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: From 1975 I worked in the railway construction enterprise in Belgrade. I went into the field in Pristina and all over the former Yugoslavia, and then in 1981 I started to work in Focatrans and this is where I worked until I was -- they made me leave. Later in 1995 I got a job at the Foca correctional facility, which was the KP Dom at the time, that's what it was called, and it's still there today. I'm still not retired, but I intend to take my retirement this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And are you able to tell us where you were when the war broke out?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: I was at home with my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And where was your house?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: Well, I had an apartment in town, but I had left and was in a village close to Foca, some 5 to 6 kilometres away from Foca, and that's where I was staying with my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The word "fled" has not been translated. Can you please tell us when you left as a refugee, when you fled, and why.

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: Well, I fled in early April 1992 because the Muslim forces were evidently arming themselves and it was obvious to all the citizens of Foca, and this part of town where I was living had a predominantly Muslim population. And then my village where I come from is an ethnically pure Serbian village, although it borders with two Muslim villages, and this is where I escaped, fled, went as a refugees in order to save my family, my wife and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And save them from what? What kind of danger were they in?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: Well, there was the danger because a couple of days before the conflict broke out the Muslim forces set up barricades, and one of them was set up in that part which leads to my village. Another barricade was set up near the medical centre in Foca. So you couldn't pass. The only people who could pass were people in medical ambulances and there was some other vehicles that were not allowed through.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the complete sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And who controlled those check-points and who decided who would pass and who would not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was told that the interpreters did not hear the complete sentence. Could you repeat the last sentence, Mr. Pljevaljcic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last sentence was that Muslim forces were at the check-points. They were armed. Some of them were wearing civilian clothing and there was a number of them wearing military uniforms, camouflage uniforms. The only vehicles that were let through were ambulances or hospital -- vehicles that were going to the Foca hospital. But the last day before the conflict broke out they were not letting those vehicles through either, so that eventually that section of Foca was completely blockaded. That was my last sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Pljevaljcic, can I ask you to speak slowly again and put a pause before you start answering the question of Mr. Karadzic. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what was the situation in the other parts of Foca in that regard?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: Well, as for other parts of the town, I think that the Serbs also put up a barricade in the direction of Cerezluk which is a neighbourhood mostly populated by Serbs; that's where the church is located, in that area, the Serb Orthodox church. That's where the Serbs put up a barricade. There were no other barricades in Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And these Serbs and these Muslims who had put up these barricades, who were they? Were they some sort of official forces? Who were they?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: Well, there were no official forces at the time, yet these were local Muslims from Foca, they were known to us, as well as the Serbs. They were also citizens of Foca. There were no other forces from outside there yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And how did the police force act, the official police forces which were a state organ?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: The official police forces did not react at all and they were not able to react to these things either because the police was divided. The town was supposed to be divided as well, in the sense of dividing the authority, the government, in the town. And they negotiated about that for a few days. The police station was already divided along the lines of the executors and floors. One floor was supposed to go to the Muslims and another to the Serbs. The executive authorities in the municipality of Foca was negotiating about the division of power in the town so that on that day before the conflict actually broke out the division was discussed, and then in the afternoon two Serb negotiators were supposed to be arrested, Mladjenovic and Bodiroga [phoen]. They managed to avoid being lynched. And then according to talk later the conflict broke out on Tuesday, and on Thursday other Serb members in the executive power and active in politics were supposed to be hijacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, we will go back to that, but I just want to ask you a little bit more about this division. Was this supposed to be a physical division or was it about forming two distinct municipalities?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: This was about forming two municipalities. It was about dividing the municipality and that's how it turned out in the end. After the war the municipality of Foca was divided in such a way that the Muslims now have Ustikolina which was before part of Foca. Now it's called Foca Ustikolina. And then the town was supposed to be divided as well; however, it would have been better if the division had actually taken place rather than what happened because some people did not wish this to happen, they did not want this division to actually occur.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there conditions -- or, how large is the territory of Foca? Was it possible to create several municipalities from that municipality?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: In the former Yugoslavia, the Foca municipality was the second-largest one, just behind Niksic, so Foca is a large municipality and it was possible to divide it. Of course not -- of course it's a large territory, it had the proper infrastructure, all the institutions could be divided, and I think that that would have been a much better solution than the one that was actually implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And in that case if each community would have had their own municipality, would it have been possible to expel anyone and would some troubles possibly have been avoided that occurred later?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: Well, any peaceful solution without expulsions, without war, without conflict would be better, and that's why I say that it would have been much better had this matter been resolved peacefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what was the position of the Serb side in Foca? What were they advocating?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: The Serb side in Foca was in a way always in a subservient position. I'm going to quote a few examples. When national parties were supposed to be have been formed - I think this was sometime in the spring of 1990 - that was when the Serbs sent out an appeal or they put a question to the constitutional court of the then-Bosnia and Herzegovina not to permit national parties from registering because the Serbs could see where this was leading. However, the answer of the B&H constitutional court was negative to the Serbs and they did permit national parties to register, they were formed, they were registered, and we all remember very well the meeting -- the rally in Foca and the flags - and we will discuss that later - so that after that, a month or two after that, the Serbs were forced to form the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was listening to this examination-in-chief and it's a totally different examination-in-chief that could have been expected. When we look at the -- when we look at the statement that the witness has actually given, there is no subject of that kind in there. So I'm -- the Prosecution did not get any notice of what the witness would be speaking about.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may respond. Ten to 12 paragraphs or 15 or more were deleted that referred to the conditions in which the Serbs lived in Foca. So now I have to get to these answers beyond questions that have to do with him personally or Focatrans that deal with the conditions of life that had an effect on eventually the outbreak of the conflict. I did not request for a viva voce examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, given that this witness is giving his evidence live and that the subject matter so far dealt with related -- are related to the background of the conflict, I would let the accused continue. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pljevaljcic, you mentioned that Muslims were arming themselves and preparing for war. How did you know this?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: Well, we knew that through various reports. I will give you some examples. Before the war broke out, police near Gorazde, near Ustipraca stopped a trailer-truck that was going to Sarajevo from somewhere in Sandzak and the goods it was carrying were suspicious -- actually, there were arms. That was when the security services centre began working in Sarajevo. The minister was a Muslim, so this was hushed up. Another example was when once the war started after a couple of days when the Muslims left Focatrans, in the compound of Focatrans there was a trailer-truck full of mortar shells but they were packed in its original packing of Badelj [phoen] cognac and that's how the shells were packed. Then the Focatrans warehouse, because the Focatrans cafeteria was located in the basement not on the ground floor, these were very large rooms and warehouses and then next to Focatrans there was an enormous railways warehouse which had stopped operating a long time ago. A lot of weaponry was found there and medical equipment, a lot of food was found there. So I think that the bulk or a large part of the weapons that came to Foca came in with Focatrans vehicles not just from Gorazde but also from Sarajevo. If I may add also, when the conflict broke out, they were working intensively on the manufacture of other types of weapons, and when the conflict actually broke out the first evening there was strong shelling of the settlement that I mentioned in the beginning, Cerezluk, where the Serbian Orthodox church is. Intensive shelling began from multi-rocket launchers and mortars and we got a little bit concerned then because you can imagine what a multiple rocket-launcher is with rockets -- large number of rockets being fired. So when the hill was captured a couple of days later, this Weber was captured and brought to Foca and you could see that it was a multiple rocket-launcher that was handmade and it was produced in Unis which is a factory which produces wires. And the Muslims were holding the post of director and head of production and a Serb was participating in the production of it, and then when he saw that he said, "Guys, I made this so it was funny for me. How did you make it you're going to prison?" And he said, "Well, I was given instructions by my chief. I don't know why this was necessary." So he produced some parts of that. He didn't actually put it together. So he made some parts of that multiple rocket-launcher.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will not ask you any further about Focatrans, but could you tell us how possible that these weapons were discovered only after the Muslims withdrew from Foca? How come you hadn't discovered it earlier?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: Well, you know how we discovered it? The police in Foca was divided and so was the police station, and if there was anything being brought in people just didn't expect it. No one expected the fighting and the conflict to be so fierce. There were stories going around. People knew that there were weapons being brought in, but somehow there was nothing done about it. People sort of expected that someone from the top would interfere and stop all of that, but unfortunately that did not happen and we know what happened afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As for those stockpiled weapons that were warehoused in Focatrans, did Serbs have access to them and were they in a position to uncover this in time?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: Well, it's quite possible that some of those weapons were hauled in by the Serbs themselves. You know what happened? I think about 104 of us were issued work permits and the director Djurid -- Murid Djuliman, he brought in another 70 Muslim labourers. Now, about ten Serbs left, they went back home, they had their own families, they had no means of living, so they were forced to come back and work with the Muslims. Now what happened? The people who remained, they worked under a special regimen there. There was something about it in the paper that was issued about it at the time, I believe it was called "Vox" and the editor was Sahinpasic, called Saja. Well, so most probably the Serbs were the ones who hauled in the weapons with the trailer-truck that was discovered because they weren't really -- they wouldn't have been able to enter the compound because was there was an officer on duty, a driver who was on duty at the gate. He was guarding and overseeing entry into and out of the compound, so no Serb would have been able to enter the perimeter in his own vehicle because at the gate itself they would have to hand-over the vehicle. And my apologies, Mr. Karadzic, but as I said most probably the Serbs brought these weapons in because of course they had a travel slip. It said on the travel slip that this was cognac that they were being -- that they were bringing in. So they didn't know that it was something quite different.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now to assist the interpreters, it says in the transcript here when we received work permits, but could you please describe to the Trial Chamber what it is that in our language the word to receive work permit means or work booklet?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: Well, to receive, to get back, our work booklet means to get a pink slip. In other words, you are fired. That's what it means.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Never mind, this is a phrase that we use, a work booklet, but the interpreters do not necessarily know it. Now, tell us, what was the connection between the firing of those 104 Serbs and the hiring of 60 Serbs and the weapons?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't 60 Serbs that were hired -- re-hired, it was 60 Muslims that were re-hired in their place. Well, you see, when we were trying to figure out later on what had happened, in fact this is what it was. The Serbs were in the way of the Muslim authorities, they were in the way of what Focatrans had in mind and their objective was to arm the Muslim population in Foca, Gorazde, and the surrounding areas, and they couldn't do it because of the Serbs. Because you can see it if you look at the Serbs who returned, who went back to work there, they simply had no insight into what type of goods were coming into the Focatrans compound and what goods were leaving it. So most probably the Serbs were an obstacle and in fact it is incomprehensible. The former Yugoslavia or even Europe had never seen a thing like that, that in a multi-ethnic society over 100 employees are fired at the same time. I believe there were perhaps two or three Muslims in that group who also were fired, but that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was the position of the police officers from various ethnic communities regarding the arming? Who was it who took part in this whole operation?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: Well, as I've said a moment ago, the police just observed the arming but did nothing about it, they didn't react, because they would have been fired. And they too could then become victims of the ethnic divisions and they could be left without work because at the time there was still one single chief of the SUP. He was a Muslim. But as I've already said at the beginning, all the plans had already been in place about the divisions. Now, the civilian authorities themselves could not prevent the arming either. Simply, they just watched what was happening wordlessly and things just went their way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about the religious communities?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: Well, religious communities had policies of their own that they pursued, and one could see what their positions were at a religious meeting that -- a rally that occurred in mid-1990s in Pijesak, that's an area in Foca. And it became clear then what the positions of the various religious leaders who had come from various parts of the former Yugoslavia were. Now, as for our rally that was at the stadium - and I'm referring -- I don't think there were any priests or any religious personalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the religious buildings, were they used in the war effort?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: Well, absolutely they contributed to the war effort, they were used, the premises. I think you can see it in one of the statements of Sahinpasic, who said that he was surprised when he found in Ustikolina in the mosque building over 100 rifles. I believe there was several other mosques. At Gornje Polje, I believe there was one. I can't recall what its name was. There was even training being organised there. The first person who was killed, the first of our men, Serbian, he was killed from the minaret, from a mosque minaret. So the Muslim religious buildings in Foca served as warehouses. The same is true of the Sajina [phoen] mosque in Donje Polje. It was used as a warehouse and he was involved in the sales of vegetables and fruit -- well, he too was involved and that mosque too was used for warehousing Muslims -- arms. Although the town itself was -- had a Muslim majority. Now, the services, the religious services, were held on Sunday, every Sunday, and I don't think you could observe anything on those occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, how many mosques were there in that general area all together, can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't tell you for certain but about four or five but I believe only two were active. In other words, the others did not have any religious service organised on their premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, was it risky to store weapons and ammunition in those facilities in the town and were there any other -- was there any other war-related equipment that was held there?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know, but in this one mosque there was so many of these anti-tank shells and I don't know where that would have come from. There was also an explosion in Aladji [phoen] mosque. There was a rumour going around when this mosque was blown up, it was sometime in early fall, I had been wounded and was in Belgrade for treatment. Now, I know that the mosque was blown up at the time. There was some 200 kilogrammes of explosives there. Now, whether the mosque was mined, or rather, blown up by the Serbs or whether it was spontaneous, we don't know, but it was a very strong explosion. Now, my place was about 200 metres away from there and all the windows were broken as a result of the explosion. But as I said, I was in Belgrade at the time so I wasn't a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, again the entire passages here is -- has nothing to do with the statement and the information that the Prosecution was notified of. It seems to me that here Mr. Karadzic tries to basically repeat the testimony of the previous witness from Foca and it has nothing to do whatsoever with the witness's evidence so far in the past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take your point, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff. Mr. Karadzic, while every detail of viva voce evidence should be notified to the other party, but I think this issue has never been discussed in his earlier statement or your notification. Do you understand that, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellency, but I believe it was discussed in detail that mosques were used as warehouses for weaponry and ammunition and other equipment. This was in paragraphs 17, 21, and I'm referring to the unredacted version. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pljevaljcic, could you just tell us one last thing. Seeing that the Muslims were arming, what did the Serbs do, did they start arming?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer, Mr. Pljevaljcic, yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This reference by Mr. Karadzic to paragraph 17 is entirely incorrect. It's basically dealing with one mosque being mentioned here and that's the Saja mosque one year before the war having had weaponry in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ustikolina.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let me see the last question -- yes -- let's leave it --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But in paragraph 21 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you remember the last question, Mr. Pljevaljcic? Can you answer the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I remember. As for arming --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I believe the Presiding Judge was referring to the previous question before this whole conversation referring to the mosques. Am I correct, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no, we leave the mosque there. Your last question seems to be this: Seeing that the Muslims were arming, what did the Serbs do? Did they start arming? That was the last question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understood and that's what I was going to answer to. There was only a reserve complement of the police. They were the only ones who armed. There were -- the Serbs also had a lot of hunting weapons and there was a warehouse not far from the town itself where the civilian Defence had its weapons, but there weren't many weapons there. Some infantry weapons and that's all. That was in the area that was under the control of the Serbs. Now, when the conflict broke out on the following day, the Serbs managed to get some of the weapons from that warehouse. The Serbs could not obtain any other weapons because the former Yugoslavia and the Army of the former Yugoslavia was nowhere near Foca. There was a barrack in Ustikolina; however, that was under the control of the Muslims. And over 80 per cent of the population probably was Muslim so that the Ustikolina barrack was under Muslim control. We didn't have any other help, any other assistance, either from Sarajevo or any place else because Foca was almost blocked totally, cut off. Trnovo was under the Muslim control, so was Gorazde. Now, after the conflict broke out, part of the weapons were obtained, the Serbs received part of the weapons, from the then-Yugoslav army. But as I said, they didn't have any infantry weapons before the conflict broke out, they did have hunting weapons, but they also managed to get some weapons when they broke into this warehouse which was not far from Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who was it who took all the weapons from the Territorial Defence that belonged to various communities and companies, local communes and companies?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: Well, the only weapons that were there were the weapons used by the MUP. They had fire-arms, automatic rifles. Now, the Muslims took their weapons. The Serbs took their weapons from these facilities. But as I said, this warehouse, the civilian protection warehouse, was in the area that was under the control of the Serbs. And they took part of that -- a part of that cache of weapons, but they didn't have a lot of weapons because the civilian protection didn't really own a lot of weapons but there were no military companies in Foca so there were no weapons within companies themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, could you tell us briefly, describe the outbreak of the conflict, who started it, how it started, who opened fire, and who was killed.

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: Well, I mentioned a bit -- I spoke a little earlier about the barricades. First they were built roadblocks by the Muslim people some three days before the conflict broke out. The first civilian victim in Foca was in Vukovina village some 12 to 15 kilometres away from Foca in the direction of Cajnice, when a woman, the wife of the late Manojlo Jankovic was killed and his daughter was wounded as they were tending to their garden. Now, later on the unfortunate Manojlo was also killed. He didn't want to open the door but they shot fire through the door and we found him dead inside. So the first victims were Serbs. Now, the first houses that were set on fire were -- and this happened a day after the conflict broke out. This happened in Foca. I believe these were the houses of a man called Kovac and then Milisav Kovacevic. There was also the house of Milisav Obrenovic and Boza Drakulic. So there were four to five houses that were in a row and they were in the area that was predominantly Muslim. Now, these houses were the first that were burnt down. The first rapes in Foca that occurred was the rape of a Serb woman who was raped before the eyes of her husband. This too was in the area that was under Muslim control and I believe that this woman testified before this Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we just please briefly go into private session so that the witness can mention the name of the victim who testified in a trial here?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that's not relevant because we have heard that before, that when one side does something bad doesn't -- that's tu quoque.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was wondering at all how this witness could know that witness testified with protective measures here at the Tribunal. Would you like us to know the name of the victim? I don't think it's necessary.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's just for credibility's sake, but the witness can explain how he knows about that. It certainly wasn't us who informed him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you coming to a close, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hopefully I can wrap-up by the end of this session.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karadzic, if I may, the first civilian casualties in Foca were Serb casualties --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- the first barricades --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no. You are supposed to answer the question put by the accused, Mr. Karadzic. If necessary, Mr. Karadzic will ask the question. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mentioned some ladies working in a field. How did that reflect on the atmosphere in Foca, the first casualties and the first fires that broke out? What kind of situation did that bring about in Foca in terms of how people felt?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: The first cases of arson and the first shellings caused panic in Foca. So the day after the first shelling there were rivers of both Serbs and Muslims who headed towards Montenegro and Serbia. You know what it's like when you spend a whole night under shells, it's a dreadful thing and nobody who has not been through that kind of an experience can possibly understand what it's like. So there was general panic that started affecting the civilian population. There were large convoys of people leaving town. Many of the Muslims took shelter in various rooms in the Serb-controlled territory where there was a Muslim minority. The civilian authorities set up guards and found people who protected these groups, but most of the Muslims fled to Serbia and Montenegro. Those who remained were secured by the Serbs. This was on a voluntarily basis. The Serbs made sure there were buses available to take these people away and I think there were over a hundred buses that were used to take Muslims to Sandzak, to Novi Pazar, and to Skopje. Many of the Muslims were put up in the surrounding villages that were Serb controlled. Over at my place there was a Muslim family with two children; they left in safety. I was actually the one who drove them there. So there was a general chaos that ensued after the first shelling and the first fires.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Just for credibility, can you give us the name of that family that you welcomed in your home for a while and then helped them to leave?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was the Kuloglija family. The lady's name was Senada, she was a court officer in Foca, and at one point fled to my village which was ethnically pure, as I said. She stayed there with her two under-aged children, two sons, one aged about 12 or 13 and the other about 7 or 8. There were other examples like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who was behind the shelling which you suggest caused chaos to arise in Foca? What date was that and what time of day exactly?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: It was the Muslims from a nearby hill just outside Foca called Sis te. They started shelling a Serb settlement called Cerezluk. They used a multiple rocket-launcher for the shelling and there was also a mortar that was used. The Serbs had no weapons at the time so they were unable to fire back at the Muslims. The next day after the shelling had stopped there was mayhem and panic in Foca. The next day infantry fighting erupted. So the shelling first started on the evening of the 8th and then the next day people were fighting using small arms. And the first fighter, Rogoljub Trivkovic [phoen] was killed in Alaca [phoen]. He was killed by a bullet fired from the mosque there. There was an initial round of negotiations that took place. I negotiated with Halilovic because the next day they started shelling the right river-bank as well of the Ceotina river. I spoke to Halilovic and I tried to reason with him. There was a phone line they were using while the phone lines were still operating, so he used that to get in touch with a Muslim colleague to plead with him to stop the shelling the right river-bank which was predominantly Serb, where there were also Muslims there. There were 33 Muslims staying in a large room in a house there. We offered them shelter there and all these people, the 33 Muslims, later safely left Foca. So Halilovic called this colleague of his on the other side who was on top of that hill and he said, "Stop shelling the right river-bank because we're all together here, Serbs and Muslims alike." And, well, one thing I can tell you, the shelling stopped, but then infantry fighting erupted in the city itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who was it who was defending and who was attacking at the time? This infantry fighting that you're talking about, what did that look like?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: Well, you know how it was. There was a part of town that was Serb-controlled, and naturally it was the Serbs who were defending that particular part of town. As for the Muslim part of town, that's on the right river-bank. As far as the hospital and the KP Dom, that was Muslim controlled and that's where the barricades sprang up and that's where the fiercest of the fighting occurred as well. The Muslim headquarters was in the Focatrans compound. After the first shelling there were many civilians who fled there to the headquarters. People were saying about 500 persons. As Serbs were advancing in terms of this infantry fighting, the Muslims were retreating towards Gorazde. So the headquarters left the Focatrans compound. People were saying there were 500 Muslims retreating along with the HQ in the direction of Ustikolina and further on towards Gorazde because they still controlled that part of the territory at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How did it come about that the Serbs prevailed although they were not as well organised and certainly not as well armed as you suggested?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: This is how it went. Focatrans caused a lot of harm to the Serbs, that's true, but this was the one instance where it actually helped, where it was useful. The Serbs could never come to terms with each other in Foca, and it was all Focatrans' fault, and then the severe beatings perpetrated by the special forces who had been sent from Sarajevo. So obviously there was a lot of determination to take Foca and to put it under control on their part. But what I'm saying is that it took a mere four -- five or six days to take Foca. There weren't really that many casualties. All together I think a total of ten casualties and that's on both sides, so very few casualties, and the Serbs were now in control with no assistance from any other quarters, not from the Serbian Democratic Party leadership, not from the JNA. The Serbs self-organised thanks to Focatrans because Focatrans, those people came to their senses, and then it was possible to organise themselves, which was unlike the Serbs in a way. And the Serbs proceeded to free the territory of their municipality. So the entire municipal territory of Foca was free in a matter of months. I'll give you an example. I was wounded on the 14th of July, 1992, at Cerva Ravna. That is what the place is called which straddles the border between Foca and Gorazde. That was in July 1992. And when Dayton came along the Serbs were still there. They never budged from that spot. They never made any incursions into Gorazde municipality at all. And the situation was like that along the entire line being held by the Serbs at the time. They freed the territory from armed bandits, from armed Muslim groups, they freed all of Foca's municipal territory and they kept it like that until the end of the war. There were two offensives launched by the Muslims trying to get it back, but Alija Izetbegovic was unable to hold on to Foca. After Foca had fallen he said he felt very bad about this, about Foca falling in particular, and that he would never be able to forgive the Muslims for allowing Foca to fall into Serb hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what about the predominantly Muslim parts of Foca, was that under control at the time as well?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: The last place that the Serbs managed to free was Tjentiste and Sutjeska. That was the last location that was liberated by the Serbs. And then they took a couple of months to cleanse the whole territory of Muslim armed units and then it was fully under control. There were incursions being launched by Muslims throughout the war, resulting in so many casualties. You know about Josanica, you know about Jabuka, you know what happened at Gornji Miljevina. Every time the Muslims launched an operation, it would result in no fewer than 60 civilian casualties on our side of the front line, people who were actually massacred.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber briefly about Josanica and all these other villages? What exactly was it that happened there?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We have now an attempt again to get tu quoque evidence in here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to respond or are you minded --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By all means. By all means, Your Excellency. We are certainly not trying to justify anyone or anything here, but events are related, there is a causal link between these events. It's not about justifying. What we need to do is try and understand what it means to kill 60 civilians in a single village and that is merely something I'm using in order to introduce the next question I have for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Since you said so, I don't understand your causal link between these events. Could you explain it to us?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By all means, Your Excellency. This is what I mean. For example, were the Serbs planning something? Was this part of the plan or were these moves caused by fear and by precedence in terms of people getting killed the day before, for example? Because what the Serb community is doing today is very much a result of what the Muslims did the day before. I'm trying to ascertain whether this was a civil war chaos or whether there was actually a plan, a Serb plan, at work here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, Mr. Pljevaljcic, this is not a question for you. Just could you just exercise your patience a bit further. Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the attack on the village of Jabuka, that is a matter from July 1992. It has nothing to do with the outbreak of the war and nothing to do with the crimes that are charged. It's basically -- it is tu quoque evidence, and it has nothing -- you cannot justify the beginning of the war and what happened in Foca with something that happened in July 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the Chamber agrees with Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff's observation as to the relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could just point out that scheduled incident 5.4 in schedule A charges a killing in the municipality of Foca that took place in July of 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Schedule -- what's the number of schedule C?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Schedule A and it's item 5.4.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How is it related to this village of Jabuka, Mr. Robinson, since you raised that issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, and I myself don't know and perhaps either the witness or Dr. Karadzic could relate that, but in any event, events which occurred in the municipality in July of 1992 were clearly relevant in the indictment. We're not even limited to the scheduled incidents. That's just an example. But I just thought it was necessary to point it out since Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff was taking the position that only events leading to the outbreak of war were relevant. So it seems to me that even absent a direct link between the two events, the fact that the indictment encompasses events in July 1992 makes Dr. Karadzic's question relevant and his point valid, that in order to understand these events it's necessary to see it from both sides, not simply the one side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You're saying that absent a direct link between these two events. And Mr. Karadzic mentioned causal links. Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Just to be very specific, Jabuka is in the direction of Gorazde, while the village Mjesaja/Trosanj is in the direction of Tjentiste, just the opposite direction, the other end of the Foca municipality. And when there were -- there occurred an attack, it can possibly have nothing to do with what happens between -- on the front line -- along the front line between Gorazde and Foca.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think a single answer by the witness can clarify the whole issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, what was your question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness mentioned that I was aware of what happened at Josanica, Jabuka, and so on and so forth. I'm aware of that but the Chamber may not be. So then I proceeded to ask the witness to tell us what happened there, because the witness himself saw fit to point out the important role that these incidents played in the overall events. That is why I asked him to elaborate on that. I know what happened there but I want the Chamber to know too. This is a link established by the witness himself in his testimony. He said that what happened there affected the further course of events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And what is your submission as to the relevance to your case?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, I was asking the witness -- the accused --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yeah, but I wanted to -- I should have done that actually earlier. The witness is listening to this submission all the time. I think it would be better if he would put off his earphones because this discussion may basically influence him.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I may speak in English too so if you need --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, it's being translated as well --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: No, no, if he removes the headphones then ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the Chamber doesn't consider the question is relevant. Could you move on -- or given the time shall we take a break now?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's a good idea. I would need another 15 minutes after the break, the same amount of time that was taken up by the objections just now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll take a break for half an hour and resume at five past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm afraid I have mention that we have to continue to sit pursuant to 15 bis for the remainder of today, and with respect to the points Mr. Robinson raised earlier today the Chamber has decided to have a hearing at quarter past 2.00 with the attorney and the representative of the Registry present at the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That means that we'll stop hearing the witness at quarter past 2.00 and continue to that hearing. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pljevaljcic, you mentioned that -- actually, first I would like to clarify this: Which part of Foca stayed outside of the Serb control and was under the control of the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: Are you thinking of the period?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In 1992, right away.

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: Tjentiste was under the control of the Muslims in 1992 then Ustikolina and a part of Slatina for a brief period. This was the part of Slatina that links on to Cajnice and Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And which part of Foca became the Muslim municipality of Foca Ustikolina according to the Dayton Accord?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: Well, that's the part of the territory facing Gorazde, so in Dayton that was conceived as Foca Ustikolina. So the Muslims did not manage to achieve their intentions regarding Foca so they were awarded this additional part, Foca Ustikolina. But that area that faces Gorazde is quite a large territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And in negotiations would the Muslims have been given a larger territory for Foca municipality?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: Well, in any case they would have because there was 1500 more Muslims in terms of the population in Foca, so they would have been awarded more. At least 70 or 80 per cent of the villages gravitating around Foca were Muslim villages. The majority of the villages were Muslim, so in any event they would have received more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And in the town itself what was the majority population?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: I think that there were more Serbs, some 5- to 600 more Serbs, and overall in the territory of Foca there were some 1500 Muslims more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, could we just make sure to make pauses between question and answer. Now let's talk about the Muslim villages that stayed under the control of the Serbs and which were cleansed of fighters, Muslim fighters. What happened to the Muslim civilians in those villages?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: All the villages around Foca which were predominantly Muslim. In the cleansing, most of the Muslim able-bodied men fled towards Gorazde. Those who stayed, they stayed a little bit closer. Because I said earlier that Foca was the second-largest municipality in Yugoslavia so those people went to the outlying neighbourhoods. Some of them went to the town neighbourhoods in Foca so that it would be easier to make sure that they were secure. I said that on the right bank of the Cehotina river there were 33 civilians, women and children. They were placed there. They spent a few days there. They would go to feed their cattle from time to time and the same thing applied to the left bank. There was a collection centre in a Muslim house, but there were guards everywhere. The authorities and the Foca Crisis Staff assigned people who guarded those families in three shifts. They guarded those civilians. There is an example in Codor Mahala. When the conflict broke out in Foca some of these let's call them volunteers or paramilitary members came in those initial first few days, some 30 of them, and one of them tried to enter Codor Mahala to get to those civilians, and he was killed by the guards that were posted there. So the Serbs had a lot of problems during those couple of days with the paramilitary members or the volunteers, whatever they were called. There was also shelter in another area and I know for a fact that civilian authorities assigned guards everywhere and that the guards were functioning and the point of the guards was precisely to prevent undesirable persons from entering those places.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned that the village civilian population sought shelter in Foca and they could go to their villages to take care of their livestock. Did they find shelter in the part of Foca that was under the control of the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: Of course they went to the part controlled by the Serb side. These shelters were all over in that section. As for Foca itself, the town was liberated in some three to four days, this is the town itself. But then there were the outlying areas around Foca that were left but this didn't take more than ten days other than the villages that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, let's clarify one thing. These guards prevented unauthorised entrances to the shelters. Did they also prevent the Muslims from going out from the shelters, Muslim civilians?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: Of course they did. Whoever, Muslim or a Muslim family, wanted to go out, they would get permission from the guards. They would seek this permission to be allowed to leave. They could go out towards Niksic, towards Montenegro, and also towards Serbia but via Montenegro through Plijevlja [phoen]. The majority of the Muslims, as I said, left in our transport, buses and so on, whoever wanted to. Those who did not want to stayed. I know a few cases. There's Dr. Zijo who stayed and he was there I think until late July or August. And then Suljo Hajric who is currently in Norway somewhere. He stayed with his wife and son and daughter, also until late July or early August. I also have a colleague who worked at the KP Dom with me. He was there until the end of August, I think. There were people, Muslims, who did not wish to leave, and they stayed there. They lived normally in the same way that we did. I think that the Red Cross helped all of those Muslim families with food and other necessities, but those who wanted to leave, they left. They were provided with transportation and nobody was expelled. I have a hard time with people saying that they were expelled. No one was expelled, but the paramilitary formations were expelled -- well, actually they were not expelled. They were fleeing in front of Serbian forces, but then they would come back and make incursions around Gorazde and Josanica and I wanted to clarify some things about that but I was not allowed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's just clarify one thing. In terms of terminology, you were going -- you were talking about departures, but what I was saying was were they allowed to leave these facilities to get food, to go to their village, take care of livestock? This is what I meant.

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: Of course they were permitted to do that. It was allowed, but villages that are 10 to 20 kilometres away from Foca, it didn't occur to anyone, Serbs were Muslims, to go up there, because it was deserted. The Muslims who were close by in the outskirts of the town, they were allowed to go. As for food, they would go to shops and whatever was there in the shops that was available. They would go out and buy these things. They lived just as the Serbs did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Other than the civilians from the villages, were there any Muslim civilians from the town itself who stayed who did not escape during the fighting?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were. There was a goldsmith. Unfortunately he died a couple of years ago. He was there throughout the whole war. There were a few other Muslims who were there. There were Muslims in our army. There was a Muslim who was killed in our ranks. He fought in our ranks. There were some other Muslims who were there throughout the whole war, men and women, and who are living in Foca to this very day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us the Trial Chamber what the difference is between those who escaped or who left -- well, I don't mean left freely to Serbia and Montenegro, but who fled to Gorazde under -- territory under Muslim control and those who dared to remain in areas under Serb control, what was the decisive factor here?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: The distinction here is that those who stayed, they accepted us normally as their brothers, let's say, and they had decided to live together with us. Those who escaped or who were expelled, they were expelled because they were armed. Those who went to Gorazde, they had the idea that they wanted to dominate in Foca, and this is something that we will see later. We can talk about that later, about these Islamic periodicals associated with "Vox" regarding the green transfers of corridor on that topic, they escaped to Gorazde and were counting on coming back and they even tried that in a number of offensives to come back to Foca and were hoping to keep Foca as a Muslim community, which is what they wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned that you found out that the Serb negotiators would be caught, members of parliament, and that they would be killed and that there was a list of sorts of more prominent Serbs who were earmarked for arrests and liquidations. How did you know this?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: I told you, we knew this on the first day, before the conflict broke out. This is when the negotiations were completed about the division of Foca. And there were two of our negotiators there, Vojislav Bodiroga and Radojica Mladjenovic there, and they just managed to avoid being lynched in the early evening. They told us this, these people are still alive and they're still living in Foca today. So the final negotiations were never actually completed, and it seems that the Muslims did not really put much effort into the negotiations because they were 100 per cent sure that Foca would fall into their hands and that things would turn out the way they planned and intended for things to happen and then the special forces when they came to Foca you could tell by what the Muslims were shouting from their balconies what it was that they were preparing for the Serbian people in Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And which year are you talking about now? Was this the intervention before the elections in 1990?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: Yes, all of this happened in 1990 before the elections when the special forces came. In fact, since the strikers' negotiations in Sarajevo, there were strikers, both Serbs and Muslims, they went to Sarajevo for negotiations to the Federal Assembly and since --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We are now in the year 1990 and we are now into the topic of the Focatrans strikers. I think that was not -- that's not relevant here in the view of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, if you have any specific observation I would like you to move on. Unless you have any specific observation, please move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to clarify whether that was that intervention and whether there was another intervention after that, but we will finish that topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pljevaljcic, what was your understanding and your evaluation of those Muslims who did not escape to Gorazde nor did they seek to cross into territory under the control of Muslim authorities but wanted to go to Serbia and Montenegro? Were these peace-loving people? How did you understand this and was the attitude of the Serbian authorities towards these people?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: Most of these people were Muslims, normal people, many people are normal. They simply voiced their desire to leave the war-afflicted areas to go to a different area. Later they came back, some of them sold their property, some of them returned, those people in the outlying areas they came back, but all those people remained on good terms with us, with the majority. Those people and most of us are sharing good mutual relations. I have an example of a person who's still alive, Muratovic who left. Sisic who went to Skopje. I gave him some money, whatever I had. They needed it. We said good-bye. We exchanged -- we kissed each other good-bye. I mean, all of these people went of their own free will.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And was any property confiscated by the authorities? I'm not talking about robberies and lootings. Those Muslims who left, did any of them experience any kind of pressure regarding the status of their property?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that. I don't know that anything was confiscated by the authorities unless you mean the paramilitary forces who would, let's say, find a vehicle and then confiscate it. That was a normal occurrence during the war, but as for the authorities or the army there was no immovable property being confiscated or mobilised.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the position of the civilian authorities, the Crisis Staff, and then the civilian authorities? What was their position and what was their conduct toward or treatment of the Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: Well, I believe they were treated fairly. I think they were treated the same way that we were treated because they were considered to be citizens, and since the Muslim military leadership had left of course the Serbian authorities, the Crisis Staff, took over and they treated them in the same way that they treated us. There was absolutely no difference in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know when the Muslims began to organise themselves militarily and do you know the name Halid Cengic and what his role was in it?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: I believe that the two key persons that were involved in the arming of the Muslims in Foca were that particular Halid and Sahinpasic, also known as Saja. They were wealthy individuals, they had money, and most of the arming was done through them. I didn't know this Halid person. I heard that he worked in Ustikolina but I didn't know him. I did know the Sahinpasic, but in any case everything had to do with these two people. He was an administrative persons or director or something like that I heard later on when the Muslims took over -- well, in any case I didn't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You didn't know Cengic?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: No, I did not personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned Sahinpasic, is that the same Sahinpasic that you mentioned earlier as the owner and the editor of "Vox," a Muslim publication?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I have no time to show you the "Vox" paper now, but could you just for the Trial Chamber -- could you tell the Trial Chamber what type of publication that was and what they issued and what this caused in -- among the Serb population?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: Well, this "Vox" magazine, I believe, or publication began coming out at the same time as the events with Focatrans, but I think officially it was established in October 1991. But this newspaper or this publication was aimed at the Muslims and they would provide guide-lines to the Muslims what they were to do. And this was consistent with what happened or what was happening at Focatrans. There were -- there was an article published. There was some ten items mentioned there as to what it was that was supposed to be done with the Serbs there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Pljevaljcic, could you please tell us one more time who it was who started the shelling and the fighting? Which side was it who started the whole thing?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: Well, I can state with full responsibility that the shelling of Foca began on the 8th of April, 1992, and that it was conducted by Muslim forces, that they shelled the town from a multiple rocket-launcher from the Siste hill and there was also or were also some mortars there. Now, on the following day the Serbs engaged the Muslims in infantry fighting because they didn't have any other weapons, and everything that transpired on those first couple of days - I state this with full responsibility - the Serbs only reacted to what the Muslims started. The first casualties were Serb. The houses of worship that were destroyed, the first ones were Serb. The rape -- the rapes that began, the first casualty was a Serb woman. And everything that the Serbs did was in reaction to what the Muslims started.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now just one other question: What were the phone lines like at the time and when did you manage to establish any kind of communication with the central authorities, the government, at Pale?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: At the very beginning and just prior to the war, we had no help from or any contact with the Serb authorities at Pale or with the army, the Yugoslav army. I've already mentioned this.
