We organised ourselves and all this thanks to Focatrans because then we came to our senses, seeing what they were doing, and we -- and the Muslims had assistance from Muslim units that came from Sarajevo, that were ordered from Sarajevo. And their job was to sow fear and show Serbs what they could expect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What were the phone lines like and were you able to get any instructions from the Serb authorities at Pale?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: Well, no. There were -- the lines were down. I believe it was only the first two or so days that the communications were still operational but I believe that this central node, the communications node was in Gorazde, and that the Muslims just broke it, they cut it off. And as for everything else, everything was down, all the lines were down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Although the witness has already answered the question. Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, basically since we started this second session, the witness is addressing issues that were neither notified in the 65 ter summary nor in the statement that we got. I just wanted to mark this point, that he's addressing all sorts of topics that the Prosecution was not aware of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you're not asking to delay your cross-examination, are you?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's definitely in the interests of justice for the Prosecution to be afforded adequate opportunity to prepare for the cross-examination, and I think I would have a basis for a request for the postponement of the cross-examination. However, in order to not disrupt these proceedings even more than became apparent this morning, I'm actually able to do the cross-examination without postponing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think you're done, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. Thank you and I thank the witness. I have no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. Pljevaljcic. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Good day to you too.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, in the beginning of your testimony you mentioned that you were spending the days of the start of the conflict in a Serb village. What was the name of this village?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: The name of that village is Orahovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when did you return to Foca?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: I returned to Foca some four or five days later when it was liberated, but as I was the company commander I was with my troops between Foca and my village, in that stretch approximately, and my village was some 5 to 6 kilometres away from Foca. Well simply, we were guarding the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And I understand that you were wounded on the 14th of July and from then onwards you were in Belgrade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you returned somewhere in 1993; right?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me address first an issue that relates to finding of combat equipment in the cellar of the Focatrans and finding of other military equipment on trucks. Can I -- I would ask that Exhibit P3033 be brought up on the screen, please. And as it is coming up -- it's only in English. We have only the English version. It is the expert report of military expert Theunens that he prepared for this case, and can we please have page 51 of this report. Can we focus a bit on the second part of the page. Sir, the military expert cites here from the JNA vojni leksikon the definitions of the TO and its structure, and it says here: "It is organised in all socio-political communities, republic, provinces, municipalities, OUR, organisation of associated labour and MZ, local communities." And a bit further down it states that it is equipped to lead armed combat independently or in co-ordination with the JNA. Mr. Pljevaljcic, Focatrans was a complex organisation of associated labour; correct?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And it had three main organisations of associated labour; correct?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: Yes, the three so-called OOURs.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And the Focatrans company was a quite significant organisation of associated labour and it had its own TO unit, did it not?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: No, Focatrans did not have their own TO unit. They -- it only had a service -- a security service of sorts, a guards service. These were five men who were armed with pistols. They guarded the gate, opened the gate and closed it, and checked who went in or out, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You yourself were a member of the TO, were you not?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: I was, but at the time it wasn't referred to as Territorial Defence. I was in reserve, so-called reserve, for an extended period of time and I attended military exercises. This was something that everyone who had completed military service would do from time to time. We were in -- at the main site and we were organised and members of these -- well, it wasn't called civilian protection really. It was called civilian battalions that would organise some parades when a general was promoted or something of that sort. And this is when these exercises were held in the area between Ustikolina and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the other place.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the civilian service or the civilian protection had some warehouses but it was only operational and it would only become active if there was, let's say, a natural disaster or something of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sir, and when you were called to your duty in what you said was not called TO but reserve TO, you would gather at the Focatrans, would you not?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: We only reported with the call-up papers that we would receive from the military section. We would have to show it at our company, which in my case was Focatrans, in order to be able to attend these exercises so that we would justify our being absent for our company. So Focatrans had nothing to do with this nor did any other company.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sir, you already mentioned that you were a company commander. You were the commander of the 3rd Company of the 5th Battalion, were you not?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sorry, who was the battalion commander?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: Boro Ivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And this battalion was part of the Foca Tactical Group; right?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have Exhibit P03354 be brought up on the screen. It should be in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sir, we have here a combat order of commander Marko Kovac of the 7th of July, 1992, and it relates to, inter alia, the area of Cerova ravna and Zebina suma. Sir, Marko Kovac was the commander of the tactical group; right?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And before that he was a JNA officer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: I didn't know him but I think he was.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And he was the commander of a unit of the JNA called Uzice Corps, do you know that?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: No, I never heard that, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We have information and evidence before this Trial Chamber that the Uzice Corps took part in the fighting in Foca when the war broke out and that the Kalinovik barracks supported this attack on Foca with artillery.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, just for the orientation it's from KDZ017, KDZ239 and KDZ379.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So it's not correct when you say it was only the local Serbs that took part in the attack, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: The only thing that is correct is that the local Serbs were involved in liberating Foca. The Uzice Corps had no way of getting to Foca because you have Gorazde between Foca and Uzice. As for Kalinovik, the distance between Foca and Kalinovik is nearly 100 kilometres. Therefore -- as for Trnovo, Trnovo was a Muslim village. Therefore, you can rule out any possibility that the artillery from Kalinovik could possibly have been lending support. As for Tjentiste and Svjetevite [phoen], it -- Sutjeska and Tjentiste remained under the control of the Muslims until that autumn, therefore that possibility can be ruled out in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Pljevaljcic, you are aware that a lot of JNA units relocated from the war in Croatia into Bosnia, including the Uzice Corps who was actually relocating from Dalmatia, did it not?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is true and I did know that. There was a single unit, I'm not sure whose, it was about five days before the clashes broke out. They simply passed through Foca and were on their way to Herzegovina. That's what people were saying. They were on their way to Bileca because there was a large military compound there, but they didn't stick around nor, indeed, did they leave any of their equipment there while they were passing through. This was five or six days before the clashes broke out and the Muslims were still in Foca. They simply passed through on their way to Herzegovina and, yes, they said at the time that the unit had originally arrived from a military compound somewhere in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sir, you also said that the SDS did not organise the fighters in Foca. It was basically the local Serbs organising themselves and the SDS had nothing to do with this. That's what you said; right?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: Essentially, yes, that's what it was like. The Serbs organised themselves thanks to Focatrans. I can't repeat this often enough. Focatrans came to their senses, as people say, and got the Serbs to finally agree about something and organise themselves and that's what happened. The SDS was the only Serb party in Foca at the time and of course they were working with the Serbs and communicating with the Serbs. So it was a synchronised effort. We organised ourselves. We cleaned up the town ourselves. Whoever returned later on was always welcome and that practice continues to this day.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And Miroslav Stanic was the first commander of the Foca military forces; correct?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: He was the president of the Crisis Staff. I think that's what it was called.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And he was the head of the SDS in Foca as well; correct?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And the Crisis Staff in Foca was situated -- the SDS Crisis Staff or the Crisis Staff of the Serbs was situated in Cerezluk, near the Orthodox church, was it not, at the beginning of the war?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me now return to the exhibit in front of us and can we please have page 4 in the B/C/S and page 3 in the English on the screen. Thank you. As you can see under the header "command post: Ustikolina, barracks," we see here: "The 1st Independent Dragan Nikolic detachment shall take part in the liberation and mop-up of Ilovaca village and beyond as part of one independent battalion." Do you see that ?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: It's difficult to see, but yes I see that. Ilovaca as a village was never liberated nor, indeed, were any attempts made to liberate it. The Serb forces got as far as Ilovaca in their effort to liberate the territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sir, let me interrupt you here. My question is: This unit, this Dragan Nikolic detachment, was led by whom?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: Dragan Nikolic himself led the detachment. He was killed on the second or third day of the clashes, I believe, so the commander was killed and the unit was named in his honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who led it after he was killed?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: After he was killed, I think Branislav Cosovic was appointed to lead the unit. These were reconnaissance units and they didn't have that many men. There was several such units in Foca. The strength depended. Some had 12 men, some 15, up to 30 at the very most.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sir, you were the vice-president of the veterans' organisation in Foca and so I assume you know a great number of veterans; correct?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: I was president of the war invalids' organisation in Foca and then later I became the vice-president of the veterans' organisation. I remained in that position until I took up my post in the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And given your knowledge of the veterans, you know that Zoran Vukovic and Radomir Kovac, Klanfa, and Janko Janic, Tuta, were part of the Dragan Nikolic detachment; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: I think, I think they were. Tuta was killed I believe at some point, and the other two are alive. I think that they were members of those units.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And Janko Janic, Tuta, was killed when an arrest attempt was conducted to arrest him for crimes he had committed, sexual assaults against women; correct?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: Well, you know, he was killed by NATO soldiers. To say that -- well, to judge someone before anything has been clearly demonstrated, I don't know if the late Tuta ever raped anyone or not, it's not for me to say. One thing is certain, he was killed during an attempt by NATO to arrest him.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And Zoran Vukovic and Radomir Kovac were convicted for rapes here by this Tribunal, rapes committed against, inter alia, women detained in partisan sports hall; correct?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: I really don't know about these things. I was never in that hall myself. I wasn't part of the security detail or anything else. That was in a totally different area. I know that they were convicted. One of them has been released and the other is still in prison. Zaga is still in prison. Was anything proven and was that why they were convicted, that is not for me to say. I know they were tried.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And as you just mentioned Zaga, that is Kunarac, the independent Zaga detachment that is mentioned here right after the Dragan Nikolic detachment. It says here: "The independent Zaga Detachment shall take part in mopping-up settled areas in the direction of the 5th Battalion's attack". So that is the unit led by Zaga Kunarac, so to speak; correct?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: Zaga Kunarac was a reconnaissance man, a scout. He had five or six men with him, no more than that. He would make rounds, reconnoitring, bringing back information. That's what he did.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned in your testimony that there were some undesirable elements such as volunteers. Is that -- are these the people you refer to or who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: No. I was referring to volunteers who came from Serbia, predominantly from Serbia and Montenegro, in other words, from other countries. There were none. There were some volunteers from Russia, I heard, in some parts of the theatre of war, but it wasn't a predominant thing. There were maybe 30 or 40 of these men from Serbia and Montenegro and they simply wouldn't stay in line, if you know what I mean. They were just dissolute youngsters who wouldn't obey any orders and they had their own groups. I think they caused probably as much harm to the Serbs as they did to the Muslims. I'm quite certain about that. The Crisis Staff in Foca could hardly wait to be rid of those so-called soldiers and I gave you that example where one of those was killed and then we faced lots of problems in the days just after that killing. They came there to help the Serbs --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand the last part of the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the last part of your answer because the interpreters didn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: Well, as I said, the volunteers who were there were not desirable from the perspective of the Serb authorities in Foca. They caused harm to the Muslims, if indeed they did. But in that case they caused as much harm to the Serbs. They certainly didn't help. They refused to place themselves under the control of the Crisis Staff. They were a law unto themselves and they waged war like that. There would be several of them in a group and if there was a crime that was perpetrated in Foca or its surroundings, it was something that they did independently. The Crisis Staff had no way of establishing control over those men. As I said Foca was the second-largest municipality in the former Yugoslavia so it was an enormous territory and it was very difficult to keep all of that under control.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sir, you spoke about the arming of the Muslims well before the war and you basically gave -- you also gave some examples. The Serbs armed themselves as well. And if I understand your evidence correctly, they started to do so after the Focatrans affair in 1990; correct?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: Well, I said the Serbs armed themselves -- many of the Serbs armed themselves when the civil protection warehouse was broken into. That was the first day after the clashes erupted. The Serbs had small arms. Those who were police reservists did and the hunters did as well. The Muslims armed themselves thanks to Focatrans because that avenue was open to them. That was their logistics --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you here, sir. We don't need to repeat. You have to listen carefully to my question. It was a question about the Serbs arming and you have already mentioned that they took over -- when a warehouse was broken in. But you say Serbs came to their senses after the Focatrans affair. This I understood to mean that they prepared for conflict; right?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: I said that they came to their senses, that they got their wits back, in a manner of speaking, after Focatrans. But his has nothing to do with anyone arming themselves. When I said getting to their senses, that means it finally dawned on them, they finally understood what was in store for them. It has nothing to do with the weapons; that's a separate story which I told you about. As for the Muslims, before the war I gave you that example involving --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you. I didn't ask you about the Muslims. I asked you about the Serbs and I would like you to stick to this question.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have now 65 ter number 24394 brought up on the screen in both languages, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And as it is coming up, it is a proposal of Commander Marko Kovac sent to Vojislav Seselj, president of the SRS to party to appoint Gojko Jankovic as Vojvoda and it's dated the 13th of August, 1993. Mr. Pljevaljcic, you know that Gojko Jankovic was one of the local military commanders; correct?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: No, he was not a commander. He was a low-level komandir. It was a reconnaissance unit numbering no more than 30 men so he wasn't a commander. By this time I was in hospital in Belgrade and I was recovering.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You know the term "Vojvoda" in the jargon of the SDS party; correct? You know what it means, a Vojvoda?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: It's not a rank. It's not a title bestowed by the SDS. This is something to do with the Serb radical party, what they refer to as the Chetnik Movement. I think the term Vojvoda belongs to them and has nothing to do with the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I may have misspoken or there was a mistranslation. I actually meant to say SRS, Serb Radical Party, so I may have misspoken. Let us see how Marko Kovac for what purpose he makes this proposal and I refer you to paragraph 2. Right after the header "explanation," he refers to Jankovic collecting weapons, organising meetings --

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: I'm not receiving interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Oh, sorry. Let's try again. If you look at paragraph 2 of this proposal under the header "explanation," it says -- it refers to Jankovic collecting weapons, organising meetings and rallies, training personnel for the struggle. Reference is also made to Jankovic's experience, having taken part in the struggle against the Ustasha in Croatia and he refers to Jankovic's special detachment with which he participated in the liberation of Foca and other places. Mr. Pljevaljcic, would that be a proper description of what Mr. Jankovic's activities were before and during the war?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: The information that he was involved in Croatia is something that I was not aware of. As for Marko Kovac's proposal for that promotion, I mean Jankovic, he was probably a good fighter. So what's controversial about that? There's nothing controversial from my perspective unless, obviously, this person committed a crime. But if he was a good fighter, if he defended his people, and if his name was put forward for the highest possible rank in the radical party, I see nothing controversial about that. I'm not for a moment there going into -- I'm sorry. I'm not for a moment suggesting that someone did or did not commit a crime. Whoever committed a crime should be held to account for that. But what I'm trying to tell you here is as far as the Foca Crisis Staff is concerned --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sir, sir, I was referring you to -- I was reading, actually, to his activities in collecting weapons, organising meetings and rallies, training personnel. That's not what he did during the war; right? It's what he did before the conflict; is that not right?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: That's not true. I'm sure about that. I know that Gojko Jankovic was a native of Foca, but he actually lived in Herceg-Novi in Montenegro before the clashes broke out, so he wasn't even seen in the area. It cannot possibly be true, therefore. He arrived with his wife and children from Montenegro, from Herceg-Novi, which is a seacoast town, and he made himself available to the Serbs in order to contribute to the defence of his native town. But it is simply not true that he was present at any of the rallies. I don't think there were any. I think there was a single rally when the party was first established and that was about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to tender this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. The witness hasn't been able to confirm anything about what's been said in the exhibit and he indicated he was in Belgrade in August of 1993 when the document was written.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: First of all, the date of the document isn't really at issue because the content of the document refers to the period when the war started and when the witness was still on the ground in this area and the witness has also confirmed that Gojko Jankovic was a -- the leader of a unit, a reconnaissance unit, and he is basically also for that purpose here proposed to become a Vojvoda. So I think there is some -- there is basis. And just to also mention, it's for impeachment purposes as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, the Chamber agrees with Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff. We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6082, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have 65 ter 40199B played. And we have -- this is the video -- sorry, it has already a P number. It has a P number. It's P03476.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You said it is part of a --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This is what we -- this is actually what we had admitted with the previous Foca witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I -- when Mr. Vujicic was here we saw part of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When you presented that you told us it is part of P3476.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That's correct. I misspoke, Your Honour. It's -- can we please have P6081. That's actually the same two excerpts that we heard with the previous witness, and I want to play -- I want to play this first little clip again in relation to what Stanic said about activities before the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That's wrong -- yeah. We need to hear the voice. Can we please try again. It worked last week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you have another topic, could we come back to this --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- clip later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The only other option I would think we have is that I could simply read what Mr. Stanic is saying --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I see no problem --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sir, we have looked at this video with another witness last Friday and I simply read to you - you cannot hear now Mr. Stanic saying this, but you can -- you should accept that this is what he is saying --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Or we have -- we can upload the transcript --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's another option, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sir, if you look at the first short excerpt that you see here a bit blown up, and Mr. Stanic is referring here to the Serbian Democratic Party leaving all political activities aside and began the self-organisation of the Serbian people and he speaks about forming eight battalions which were led by some of the Serbian reserve officers and he refers to a particular event of a battalion being lined up and inspected in June 1991. Sir, this is what Mr. Stanic says about how the Serbs prepared for the conflict and he speaks of June 1991.

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. As for battalions forming in 1991, that's something that I don't know anything about. There's no date here even. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The date is June 1991, at least for the inspection of this battalion.

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: What Stanic stated after the beating of the Serbs, that is okay, but that the battalions were formed in 1991 that's something that I am not aware of. I was part of the 5th Battalion but it was not formed in 1991. This is an error.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we focus a bit further down on that same page for the second excerpt. And, Mr. Pljevaljcic, you have only two lines here, the two last lines that you can see here and we need then the B/C/S the next page. And as you can see, he is again referring to the Serbian military organisation being prepared a year before and he mentions here the first commanders --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second now. I'm not sure -- I was told that there's no second page -- yeah, the second page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: There is a second page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I -- I actually wanted to mention this when the first clip was shown. Can we please know why Mr. Stanic said it was strong? Why was it redacted? What is Stanic talking about? What was strong? That's part of the statement by Stanic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it's -- the Prosecution only offered that part --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We offered both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But Mr. Karadzic was referring to the redacted part.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Oh, the redacted part is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it Mr. Karadzic has access to the whole part, doesn't he?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, he has. And, actually, I have omitted to mention it, Mr. -- when it comes to this second part Mr. Stanic was referring to the Muslims and the Muslim forces being strong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: "It was strong" refers to the Muslims. Yes. I omitted to say that, sorry. I thought it was in here.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could have the number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The entire --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand the explanation, but what I was told that the Registry can't upload the second page. If we collapse English, then can we upload the second page for the benefit of the witness since we have read the English page.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, and I actually can read from the entire -- the entire version of this Stanic interview. It's a question -- sorry. The questions that was redacted but can and should be actually in there. The question of the host was: "Your response to the Muslims had to be swift because as we all remember the SDA party of democratic action was strong in Foca at that time." That is something that the host put to the -- to Stanic and then there is this Stanic answer. Perhaps we should upload a new version where this particular question is seen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, before she does that would it be possible to give us the 65 ter number of the unredacted version so we can follow these parts? I know it's been disclosed to us, but we don't really know where to find it at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could it be done during the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, we actually have it right here at hand, and it is 40199. That's the entire tape and the entire transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sir, here you see again the reference to the preparing of the military organisation of the Serbian people a year before, and then there comes a list of commanders mentioned, the first were commanders. And among them is Gojko Jankovic. And he is mentioned here next to Boro Ivanovic and you said that he was the commander of your battalion, the 5th Battalion, and he is mentioned here next to Pero Elez, another commander of a battalion. So Gojko Jankovic is mentioned here among the first commanders. You see that?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: I can see that but something is not quite clear to me here. There is this Radmilo Pljevadzic there. He was not a commander of any kind. He became the commander of the intervention platoon only after I was wounded and year after the conflict broke out, actually, so something is not quite clear to me here. But again, I am saying that as far as what is here, there was Boro, he was the commander of the battalion and then perhaps -- well, as for Cosovic and this Zivanovic, as for Gojko Jankovic, these were all komandirs, not commanders; that's the difference. Perhaps you don't see that distinction. They were komandirs of reconnaissance units. As for the statement by Miro Stanic, Miro Stanic and the Serbs could see that it was no joke and that after this ruthless attack on the civilian population of the Serbs, it's normal that the Serbs headed by Miro Stanic decided to self organise and to defend themselves. As for help from outside, we didn't get help either from the Pale leadership or from the Yugoslav People's Army, no help. We organised ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned a bit earlier ago that you did not know about these kind of activities, when they occurred, so you don't know who assisted Mr. Stanic in doing all this; is that not right?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: I was not a battalion commander so I wasn't really meant to know that. I don't know if the others knew it. I don't know if this is what the Crisis Staff did when forming its units, the Foca Crisis Staff. I think it numbered 15 members. So probably they were working on appointing commanders and on forming units. But it was all with the objective of defending or protecting the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sir, while you don't know matters that occurred on the Serb side before the outbreak of the war, you provided a great deal of detail in relation to the Muslims, what they were doing. That's hearsay, right? That's not what you really saw. This is what you read, that is what was rumoured, and that is what people would be speaking about; correct?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: No, it wasn't quite like that. I experienced the Focatrans. I experienced the barricades that were erected in Foca. I had personal experience with that because we had to go to bring this girl, a 10-year-old girl, from the late Jankovic who was wounded and her mother was killed. We had to bury the mother. I mean, these were all things that I experienced personally. I'm not talking just off the top of my head. I experienced the burning, the torching, of the Serb houses. It's true, I didn't see the church in Jabuka burn because it's far away, it's 50 kilometres from Foca, but I knew that it was set on fire and not only was the church torched but some 50 civilians were killed there as well and it wasn't the Serbs that killed them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sir, in your evidence here in the court, you referred to Muslims that fled to their Serb neighbours to be safe; correct?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: You mean Serbia Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, you -- sorry. I understood your evidence that while still in Foca Muslim villagers or Muslim neighbours in Foca fled to the Serb neighbours to be safe; correct? You gave a few examples and you yourself also helped and accommodated such neighbours, Muslim neighbours.

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: That's correct. I said that the Muslims had gone to safe places -- actually, the Serbs made it possible for them to seek shelter and they provided security for them. This was in places where the population was mixed or where the Muslims were in a minority. In places where the Muslims were in a majority, they held that part of town until the Serbian forces liberated that part as well. When the majority Muslim-populated parts of town were liberated, Muslims, particularly the able-bodied men, left for Gorazde. And the civilian population that remained behind were taken care of, taken to secure places and later were permitted to leave, to go to Serbia or wherever they wanted.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You also described how you helped a Muslim -- Muslims out of Foca, remember that? You gave an example of this.

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: I did, yes. This was an outlying neighbourhood of town and there were 33 Muslims placed there. They were some three days in that place and then later they left, they went safely towards Montenegro. There was another village bordering on Orahovo. It's a village by the name Subi Suljci and when the village was supposed to be cleansed, if I can put it that way, from armed Muslims, the able-bodied Muslim men from those villages had already left for Gorazde. I personally went to that village with another two soldiers. We sat in Asim Memic's house. We sat with his daughters-in-law, his grandchildren. We had coffee. They said they went to Gorazde. I said, Why did they go? We can all live together. If anybody's armed or whatever, if there are any armed formations -- I mean there was no need, so that's how it was. And so those people from that village of Subi Sulci withdrew later. Some 15 days or a month later they withdrew to Gorazde. Nobody was harmed. That was their decision to go like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But what I understand from your evidence is that Muslims needed help to get out of Foca, help by their Serb neighbours; right?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were given help. We provided help. We organised buses and whoever wanted voluntarily to leave the town -- actually, it was their request, their wish, to go to seek shelter to get away from the conflicts between the Serbs and the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned that when Muslim villages were cleansed from Muslim fighters, the civilian population was taken to locations in Foca for safe-guarding to protect them also. And in this context, or rather, we also mentioned here the villages of Trosanj and Mjesaja. There's evidence before this Court that this village was totally burnt down, that the men of the village were killed and the women were detained in Buk Bijela, Foca high school, and partisan sports hall and they were not protected; on the contrary, they were raped by men that we mentioned this morning, including also Gojko Jankovic. Isn't that what happened in Foca or would you not know that?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: I don't know about this other thing -- well, in my statement I never said that. I didn't say anything about Trosanj, Mjesaja. I am hearing of that for the first time. That's not my testimony. Actually, it's quite the opposite, as far as I'm concerned. I never said that. I don't know where you got that from.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I have actually mentioned the evidence that is before this Court, and it's actually from July 1992 so I was wondering whether that's -- you do not know about this because you were not here -- you were not there at that time but you were in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: I was in Belgrade, but actually that's quite on the other side in relation to where I lived. I told you about the right bank of the Cehotina river and the right bank of the Drina River. That's where my battalion was. As for Trosanj, I don't know. I think that the Foca Crisis Staff, its order was explicit. The civilian population was to be protected. But since the civilian population, the villages were far from Foca, this -- they had to come down to places where we could provide security which could be monitored. I know where this village of Trosanj is more or less. It's far from Foca. You would need a whole unit located up there in order to secure the population, or Tjentiste, that's more than 50 kilometres away. So this was done. And if any of the civilians remained, they were taken care of in Foca in these several locations. These people, men and women, were brought and accommodated in KP Dom as well, a number of them. I don't know whether some people were missing or not missing from the KP Dom, I mean I don't really want to get into that. But the objective of the Crisis Staff was to accommodate -- provide accommodation for the civilian population --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you here. As you don't know -- as you were away from Foca from the 14th of July onwards, I understand perfectly well that you may not know about Trosanj and Mjesaja and the details of that, but does that not also mean whatever you say about this period, that is, the voluntary departure of people, the protection of people in certain localities in Foca, that's all hearsay and you cannot confirm any of that because you were not there. Isn't that what it was?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: What I was able to confirm for you I confirmed, but I cannot confirm anything that happened in September in 1992 in Tjentiste because I heard that Tjentiste was liberated only in August or September of 1992 so I cannot say what was happening up there. I was fighting for my life at that time in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll continue after the break if you have any re-examination, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a few, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll resume at 1.25. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.40 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Pljevaljcic, just a few questions and I hope we'll be done soon. On page 55 my learned colleague, Madam Uertz-Retzlaff, asked you about the participation of the Uzice Corps in the attack on Foca. Could you tell us who it was who was attacking Foca and who was defending themselves from Foca.

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, the Uzice Corps had absolutely nothing to do with Foca nor was it anywhere near that area. As I've already said, the shelling of Foca began and it was the Muslims who were shelling it, and there was no other attack except in the following, in the ensuing, days some infantry fighting came about. But the Uzice Corps had nothing to do with Foca. It didn't take part in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pljevaljcic. What I would like you to clarify for us is this: Were there any Serb forces from outside Foca that attacked it and who were the attackers and who were the defenders of Foca?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: There were no forces from outside of Foca that attacked Foca. On our part I don't know if there were Green Berets or paramilitary units on the Muslim side, but as for Foca it was attacked by the Muslims and it was defended by Serb volunteers, Serb patriots from the town of Foca who managed to defend it and who liberated it. That is the fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to ask you now about artillery. Now, mention was made here that there was artillery taking part in the attack on Foca. Now, whose shells and whose bombs fell on Foca?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: Well, the first shells that fell on Foca were Muslim shells and this went on the first night, and then on the following day there was a multiple rocket-launcher and there was some mortars. So these shells were the first shells that struck Foca and this went on from around 10.00 p.m. up until sometime after midnight or around 1.00 a.m., so that the next day there was panic in Foca. As for shelling, there was no shelling in Foca. There were only -- there was only infantry fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, on page 57 the learned Madam Uertz-Retzlaff said the Crisis Staff of Foca and then she added the SDS Crisis Staff of Foca. Was this Crisis Staff a party organ or a municipal body? Was it -- were the members of it party people or municipal officials?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: Well, there were no party people in the Crisis Staff -- well, there was perhaps one of the members of the Crisis Staff which was a municipal staff was also a member of the SDS, but it was a municipal staff and it was established by the municipality once the negotiations fell through. Now, half of the representatives in the municipality were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 60 I'm afraid that your full answer is not reflected. Did you say there that these volunteers --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: As you have seen, Ms. Gustafson and I, we have changed the seat, but that's why I have to interrupt you because you can't see me so well anymore. I think when he now refers to -- in this way to certain things that the witness had said or may not have said, I think he has to formulate it in a -- not in a leading way. When you see here: I'm afraid that your full answer is not reflected, I think he should ask the question that he find the answer is missing to rather than citing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He was about to quote the transcript page. Should we see how he formulates his question, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, I'm only afraid that it will be already giving the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us see. What is your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I could have intervened at the time in the transcript, but I didn't want to interrupt. But I can read out a portion of the answer and then ask the witness what it was that he had also said but was omitted if that's how you would prefer it. That's page 60, lines 7 through 10. May I read it out, the witness's answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is what your answer was: [In English] "The Crisis Staff in Foca could hardly wait to be rid of those so-called soldiers and I gave you that example where one of those was killed and then we faced lots of problems in the days just after that killing. They came there to help the Serbs." [Interpretation] And then you said something else - and that can be checked - to the effect: We came there to help. And you -- could you just finish your sentence, please.

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, when this man, this volunteer, was killed - if I can call him that - we had serious problems with these volunteers, we Serbs. And they said we came here to help you defend yourself and you are killing us, something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That was not reflected in the transcript so that's all I wanted to clarify. Now on page 61 my learned colleague -- my learned friend Madam Uertz-Retzlaff said -- mentioned the Foca and she said that the arming of the Serbs began in the 1990s -- in the 1990 -- the year of 1990. Was that the case?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: Well, certainly not. I told you already about the year of 1990. The arming of Serbs began and most Serbs armed themselves - I have to repeat this one more time - on the first day of the breakout of the war which is when they broke into depots of Territorial Defence and found some infantry weapons there. There were no other weapons. There was no artillery. There were no bombs, no hand-grenades, no shells. There was only -- there were only infantry weapons. So most Serbs armed themselves then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. I just want to ask you one other thing to do with the interview with Mr. Stanic. I don't know exactly when it was that he gave this interview. Now, was it customary for local people to brag to sort of claim the credit for something that people did to claim the credit for themselves?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, that was quite common there and there's something that's not really clear to me in this report of Mr. Stanic's. Now, if you know Mr. Stanic - and I know him well - he's a very peaceable, peace-loving, quiet man. And to him a good soldier would be a commander. So that's the difference. Now, he would refer to any good patriot, any good fighter, good soldier, a commander. Now, most of these names -- most of these people whose names are mentioned there, most of them were not commanders at all. So this statement of his or this interview of his, he just tried to embellish things a bit because the Serbs were the ones who freed Foca. And he as the chairman of the party probably felt that there was some credit for him too to claim in this situation. So he was probably just embellishing a little and bragging a bit.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I wonder whether "embellish" would be translated bragging -- more properly "bragging" than "embellish." [Interpretation] Because the witness said that he was bragging.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is there much difference? We noted your observation, but please refrain from making -- asking leading questions. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, on page 72 you were asked about help you -- about the help that the neighbours, Serb neighbours, provided to their Muslim friends and how they helped them leave there. Now, what was the position of the authorities? Do you know that there was a time when the authorities tried to prevent anyone from leaving, so either side?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: I know that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Another leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The previous was already but I ignored it, but this is again leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Agreed. Reformulate your question, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was the position of the Serb authorities in Foca vis-a-vis the departures of either Serbs or Muslims from Foca?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: As for the -- both the Muslims and the Serbs leaving - and we haven't mentioned here something earlier but I think I did - that Serbs too were leaving. But as for the Serb authorities in Foca, they never tried to prevent anyone from leaving voluntarily. They assisted them in that; however, they tried to appeal to people not to leave. They said that they would try and provide everyone the protection they required, and that was the case with everyone who stayed behind. I told you of instances where people stayed behind. They spent the entire war together with the Serbs. There were also those who left toward the end of 1992 and then returned later on. There's still people who worked with me. For instance, there is a colleague at KP Foca where he left in 1992 for Turkey. He was -- this was facilitated by the Serb authorities at the time, but he returned together with his families. So the Serb authorities made it possible -- facilitated everyone who wanted to leave. They facilitated their departures. But the same applied for everyone and they allowed the Muslims everything that they allowed the Serbs. It was a difficult time. It was war time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we now briefly look at P2642. This was before your wounding, you were still in the unit. Could we please have that document P2642. While we are waiting for the English version, would you please take a look at the first page, the cover page [indiscernible]. Read it to yourself, Mr. Pljevaljcic.

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Next page, please, the first page in its entirety and then let's move on to page 2. Tell me when you're done, please.

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: Well, it's all just the way it is stated here. All those who wished to leave were allowed to leave safely and transport was provided. Those who wished to stay were allowed to get on and have a dignified existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. So this document, to the best of your knowledge, reflects the actual moves made by the Serb authorities in Foca, does it not?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, leading again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is the relation between this document and what actually happened?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: Well, I've never set eyes on this document before, but everything that I said during my evidence is entirely in keeping with what the document states and yet I've never seen it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The issue of the Muslims arming themselves was raised as well. I would like to ask you the following: You said you knew Sahim -- Sahinpasic, Sajo, and you also heard of Halid Cengic. What sort of reputation did these two people enjoy, in a legal sense, the legality of their behaviour?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I did not address these personalities and I did not address this topic of their involvement in arming, whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm trying to save time and this is a Prosecution document. Perhaps it's not known -- I'm sorry, it's a Defence document. The thing is Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff talked about rumours back in 1991 about Muslims arming themselves. I have a Muslim document here D299, which states exactly the opposite. It's a Muslim document produced by the Muslim security service --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I'm not sure whether we heard about rumours about Muslim arming. Did you ask any questions about that, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I actually put to the witness that while -- because he was not there and he would not know that, and that's what he was relying on was hearsay and rumours. I used the word "rumours," that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were those rumours or do you have information indicating that the SDA was arming the Muslims in Foca and organising them in a military sense?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: Those weren't rumours, that's for sure. If you take the case of that truck full of weapons in Foca and once the clashes had broken out there was a truck full of weapons that was stopped at Focatrans, and there was a whole arsenal, a cache of weapons in the Focatrans canteen. And if you take the whole of Gorazde which was surrounded - as this Court claims - and everybody in Gorazde was armed to their teeth, well you can imagine where the weapons came from and when did the weapons arrive. Well, it had to be at some point earlier on, didn't it? How could Gorazde have possibly been surrounded by the Serb forces and yet they were all armed to their teeth over there? Well, the weapons didn't just fall from the sky and land straight in their lap, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D299, please. Can we have that in e-court. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please focus on this. This is the BH security administration. Can we please have the final page of this document just to see who signed it. This is the 17th of July, 1993. Fikret Muslimovic, chief of security. Can we please go back to page 3. I'd like to read to you a portion of the document: "Sahinpasic is a private tradesman from Foca and a delegate to the citizens' council and Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Cengic is an accountant at the Mlin RO work organisation in Ustikolina and town councillor in the Foca. From the time they came to power having gathered around themselves their family and friends they started with all kinds of fraud and smuggling which brought them huge amounts of money. The increasingly complex political situation and deteriorating inter-ethnic relations during 1991 played into their hands, since arms smuggling was flourishing and they are doing nothing to appease the situation but were on the contrary inciting it with their actions and political activity." The last sentence said: "The rifles that Sahinpasic and Cengic are selling are being sold for 1.200 to 1.500 German marks. According to some intelligence 5.200 rifles came to Foca via the SDA which Sahinpasic and Cengic sold. What about these quantities? Was that what they obtained before the war? So were these weapons being sold during the war or prior to the war?

utterances.speaker: TRIVKO PLJEVALJCIC
utterances.text: I'm sure the information is trustworthy and accurate. The information comes from one of their documents that was signed by one of their own. It's not just that people were saying that they were arming themselves; it was what was actually happening and all the facts point to that conclusion. Where did the Muslims get their weapons both in Foca and in Gorazde? It was an open secret in Foca and Ustikolina that the mosque at Donje Polje where Sahinpasic had his warehouse was full of weapons. And it's true that rifles were being sold to the Muslims and they would pay in excess of 1.000 German marks per piece. All the Serbs and all the Muslims in that area knew that; it was no secret at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The previous document P2642 -- no, actually, it's the present document not the previous one. Is it correct that ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, just for your benefit I'm asking this. This document has already been admitted into evidence and the witness does not know specifics based upon his experience. What would you get from this witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, I just wanted to know whether the document was accurate in this witness's experience. He [indiscernible] addressed that and the OTP tried to challenge that, so that's why I included that in my re-examination. Nevertheless, I am now wrapping up and I would like to thank the witness for his evidence here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Unless my colleagues have a question for you, Mr. Pljevaljcic, that concludes your evidence. On behalf of the Chamber I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you're free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is the next witness ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you think it's worth starting in the remaining 15 minutes? That's up for you to decide of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By all means, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mijanovic. Please take a seat and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Mijanovic.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you as well, Mr. President. I wish you all the best.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we please both make pauses between our questions and answers in order to give the interpreters a chance to catch up and to make sure everything was accurately recorded. Did you make a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have 1D07029 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you have that in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you read the statement and sign it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is the statement an accurate reflection of your words?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to ask you all the same questions today that you were asked during the interview for the statement, would your answers essentially remain the same?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Essentially, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will now -- or rather, I will be tendering this statement summary under 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it there's no associated exhibits, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Ms. Gustafson?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll receive this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D2773, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But can we please keep this in e-court because I will have a question later on to clarify something. I will be reading out the summary in English now. [In English] Slavko Mijanovic was born in Ulog, Kalinovik municipality, BH. He completed his secondary education and graduated from at faculty of architecture and urbanism in Sarajevo. After the multi-party elections in BH in the autumn of 1990, he was appointed deputy secretary to the secretariat for urban planning, housing and public utilities in Novi Grad municipality in Sarajevo. Slavko Mijanovic noticed at the beginning of April 1992 the entrance to the municipal building in Novi Grad was guarded around-the-clock by armed Muslim reserve policemen. He was aware that he was being followed by the Muslim security services because he was a Serb and although he made a complaint about this, nothing changed. The security situation deteriorated and at the end of April Slavko Mijanovic resigned from his job, moved from his flat, and relocated his family to Montenegro and moved himself to Ilidza, neighbouring municipality, to work at the war time commission. Serbian and non-Serbian residents left Ilidza and many Serbian refugees moved to the territory from Muslim-controlled areas of Sarajevo. This rapid movement of people meant it was necessary to place the responsibility of flats and accommodation under the control of the municipality. The Ilidza authorities did not expel non-Serbs. They moved out of their own accord and some remained in Ilidza throughout the war. In July 1992 a commission for the distribution of flats for temporary use was founded and rules of procedure were adopted in relation to the housing situation. The commission compiled a priority list pursuant to the rules and written submissions received. The priorities set out in the rules were respected and adhered to. The decisions assigning flats for temporary use contained clauses not allowing the tenant to acquire ownership of the flat and placing a duty on the tenant to care for the flat and the property inside. The commission encountered considerable difficulties with the work it carried out due to the constant war operations, local residents unlawfully taking occupancy of abandoned flats or temporary residents stealing property. Ilidza maintained contact with the authorities and organs of Republika Srpska during the war and no instructions or orders were issued by the authorities to expel or carry out ethnic cleansing of the Muslims or any other non-Serb population in the territory or to limit or remove a person's human rights and freedoms or carry out any other inhumane conduct. And that would be the summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mijanovic, I would like to ask you something about paragraph 14 on page 3 of your statement. Perhaps we can look at it in e-court. I know, but I don't know if it's clear to the others, in paragraph you say in the last sentence: "Gun-shots could often be heard from the settlements of Mojmilo, Boljakov Potok, and Buca Potok during the night." So this is before the war broke out in the course of 1991. Whose settlements are these?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: These are majority Muslim settlements, Bosniak settlements. I don't know anymore which term to use.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't have any more questions for you at this point, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mijanovic, your evidence in chief in this case has been admitted in writing and you will be now cross-examined by the member of the Office of the Prosecutor. Yes, Ms. Gustafson, you have about ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For today.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Mijanovic.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon and all the best to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to also thank you for agreeing to meet with the Prosecution yesterday and I'd like to start by just confirming some of the things that you said yesterday in the presence of myself and an investigator from the Office of the Prosecution. The first matters relate to paragraph 4 of your statement, where you explain that at the end of April 1992 you went to Ilidza and provided security for the municipal building where the Crisis Staff and the military command had their offices. And I'd like to clarify that your role at the municipal building was, in fact, to call people to meetings of the Crisis Staff essentially; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: It is correct that I did not secure the building but was on duty in the building, on call next to the telephone on duty there. I picked up the phone and as per the orders of the representatives of the Crisis Staff or the war commissioner office I scheduled meetings of the war commission.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And the person from the Crisis Staff who was in general giving you these orders to schedule meetings was Mr. Prstojevic; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you also clarified yesterday that you personally did not attend any meetings of the Ilidza Crisis Staff or Ilidza military command; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you also clarified that you didn't take part in any combat operations and had no role in co-ordinating or commanding any police or military operations in Ilidza; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: I was never militarily engaged during the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you confirmed that Mr. Prstojevic remained the president of Ilidza municipality throughout the war and for a period of time after the end of the war; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And now I'd like to turn to paragraph 6 of your statement where you claim that the authorities of the Serbian municipality of Ilidza and their organs did not expel non-Serbs and that they moved out of their own accord and in an unorganised manner. And in that respect I'd like to go to P2308, please. This is a report from the 20th of September, 1993, from the Ilidza public security station to the RS Ministry of Internal Affairs and the security services centre Sarajevo. And if we could turn to page 2 in both languages. The second full paragraph it states that at the beginning of 1991 during illegal meetings organised by Tomislav Kovac, who was then the commander of the Ilidza public security station, policemen of Serbian nationality were informed that the war option for realisation of national interests was being increasingly promoted. A few lines down it says that it was also agreed that intense activity should be undertaken to arm citizens of Serbian nationality and armament was transported from Ravna Romanija, Pale, Sokolac, Kalinovik, the village of Nedavici, Trnovo, Torsici [phoen], Hadzici, Jusuf Jonlandzic [phoen] Barracks, Lukavica, and Nedzarici. First, were you aware of these illegal meetings organised by Mr. Kovac or these intense arming activities of Serbs referred to in this report?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: In early 1991, as it states here, I was in the Novi Grad municipality not in the Ilidza municipality area, so I couldn't have known even if this was so.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And if we could go to the next page in both languages. And now they're talking about activities in 1992 and the second-last paragraph states: "All detained Muslims were thoroughly interrogated in order to extract useful information regarding their intentions. Repressive measures undertaken against them for various reasons resulted in them increasingly fleeing and moving out of this territory." Now, in relation to your claims about the manner in which Muslims left the territory of Ilidza, were you aware of the fact that the Ilidza SJB was taking repressive measures against Muslims resulting in them increasingly fleeing and moving out of the territory?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: The Malaleja [phoen] command of the Crisis Staff or of the war commission, however you want to refer to it, I got there in mid-May and then the tram were still -- the trams were still running between the Ilidza and Bascarsija stops during that period. And anybody who wanted to move out could have done so. People could also move in to Ilidza if they wanted. And then sometime in mid-May this was not possible anymore because the town was sealed and the inside, meaning that the territory or actually the --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: -- federal part or the Muslims -- yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you but your answer is not really responsive to my question which was simply whether or not you were aware of the fact that the Ilidza SJB was taking repressive measures against detained Muslims resulting in them freeing from the territory?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MIJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Should I stop there, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Mijanovic, the Chamber has another matter to deal with for today, so we'll adjourn for today for the purpose of your testimony. We'll continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You are advised not to discuss with anybody else about your testimony. Do you understand that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mijanovic. You may be excused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably before going into private session I think I can safely note this. The Chamber is seized of certain confidential motion, and in order to resolve the issue in an efficient and expeditious way, the Chamber has invited an attorney for a witness and the representative of the Registrar. So could those two persons introduce themselves for record.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Stephane Bourgon representing the witness Dragomir Milosevic. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. OSURE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Anna Osure representing the Deputy Registrar and the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. The Chamber will go into private session for the remainder of this debate.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The hearing is adjourned.
